papers.title: Selective Admissions in Nursing Homes: Evidence from a Randomized Audit Study
papers.abstract: It has been widely documented that patients in the US who are associated with disadvantaged demographics receive care at lower quality nursing homes. To understand the role that selective admissions may play in contributing to this pattern, we conducted a nationwide audit study of the impact of patient race, payer, and medical condition on responses to about 5,500 availability inquiries sent to about 3,000 nursing homes. We find 10-15% lower availability for Medicaid patients compared to private-pay patients and for patients with Alzheimer’s disease compared to those without; these availability gaps generally increase with nursing home quality. We find no statistically significant evidence of differential availability by race. To quantify the implications of these selective admissions practices, we embed the audit study results in a model of constrained nursing home choice. We estimate that if, counterfactually, Medicaid patients had the same choice sets as their private-pay counterparts, they would attend higher quality nursing homes on average, but the private-Medicaid gap in quality would be reduced by only 5-10%. Our results suggest that supply-side availability differences by payer are widespread, but that they are unlikely to be the primary factor behind the observed gap in quality of nursing homes attended.

papers.title: The Value of (Sub) Specialization: Evidence from Oncology
papers.abstract: We estimate the returns to specialization in medical oncology, in which subspecialists focus on specific cancer types. Using 2.2 million Medicare chemotherapy episodes from 2008–2020, we instrument for subspecialist access with differential distance to cancer-type-specific subspecialists versus general oncologists. Access to a relevant subspecialist reduces three-year mortality by 4.5 percentage points (10 percent), without increasing Medicare spending or measured provider fragmentation. Subspecialists also increase the use of newer therapies and diagnosis-specific clinical trials. These findings show that specialization raises productivity when expertise is closely matched to the task.

papers.title: The Impact of Silver Loading in ACA Health Insurance Marketplaces
papers.abstract: In 2017, the federal government ended payments for cost-sharing reduction (CSR) subsidies for the Health Insurance Marketplaces created by the Affordable Care Act. Rather than uniformly increase Marketplace plans’ premiums to offset the loss of these payments, over 40 states responded by silver loading—only increasing the premiums of silver plans to which CSR subsidies apply and premium tax credits are tied. Silver loading was intended to increase the affordability of Marketplace coverage by increasing premium tax credits and thereby enrollment, though the literature lacks causal estimates. Furthermore, Congress is considering reinstating CSR subsidy funding, effectively undoing silver loading. We use panel data on 2015-2021 Marketplace health plan premiums and enrollment in 12 states from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to estimate silver loading’s effects using contiguous county-pair models. We find that silver loading functioned as intended, lowering the cost of Marketplace coverage and increasing enrollment by 8-14% among subsidized Marketplace enrollees with incomes between 250% and 400% of the poverty level. We project that Congress ending silver loading would decrease Marketplace enrollment by at least 330,000 enrollees in 2027.

papers.title: College Success: Understanding the Roles of Financial Aid, Loans, Preparation, and Incentives
papers.abstract: Over the past four decades, the earnings gap between college graduates and non-graduates has widened substantially, prompting interest in policies aimed at promoting higher education among low-income students. A key challenge for these policies is the high college dropout rate. This paper develops a dynamic model of college enrollment and completion with rich individual heterogeneity to assess how various factors influence college attendance, dropout, and graduation. We estimate the model using data from longitudinal surveys, results of quasi-experimental studies on grant aid, and large-scale randomized controlled trials. We use the model to simulate the effects of tuition subsidies, college loans, financial incentives, and increased pre-college skills on attendance and completion. We find moderate effects of most unconditional financial policies on attendance, with small effects on completion conditional on attendance. By contrast, some merit-based incentives, such as forgiving student loans upon receipt of a bachelor’s degree, have substantial effects. However, this type of policy and other financial subsidies accrue even more than the others to students from relatively wealthy backgrounds. Overall, it appears infeasible to design a financial aid policy that is simultaneously effective in raising attainment and fiscally progressive. By comparison, we find that the greatest potential for increasing attainment could come from better preparing students for college.

papers.title: Implications of Policy Interventions on Eliminating Gender Gaps
papers.abstract: This paper studies policy interventions intended to eliminate gender differences in labor market outcomes, principally wages. Because gender is an individual attribute rather than a manipulable treatment, the ideal experiment of randomly assigning gender to evaluate its effects is infeasible. Policies that remove gender labels from the employment process are the closest feasible counterpart. We quantify both the intended and unintended consequences of the policies through simulated interventions of an estimated equilibrium model of statistical discrimination with dynamic choices of education and labor market participation. In the short run the policy that requires gender free applications in the market for skilled labor eliminates wage gaps but once education choices respond the effects are attenuated. A more comprehensive policy that enforces gender free compensation reverses the wage gap in skilled markets and eliminates it in unskilled labor markets, even once education adjusts. These interventions impact college rates, the college premium gap and participation rates as well. The final section studies these interventions using a difference-in-differences (DID) approach to analyze the simulated data. With education fixed, the DID method recovers the policy effects but this is not the case once education adjusts, reflecting the effects of the intervention on both treated and control groups through equilibrium adjustments in beliefs.

papers.title: Representation, Innovation, and Product Adoption
papers.abstract: During research and development, firms must decide which types of individuals to engage in developing and testing their products. We investigate how lowering the cost of including one group shapes its representation, subsequent innovation, and product adoption. In 2000, Medicare expanded coverage of clinical trial costs for elderly trial participants, a historically underrepresented group in drug development. This policy increases representation: trial sponsors expand trial eligibility to include elderly participants and increase the share of elderly participants. We find an immediate and large increase in the number of clinical trials for diseases common among the elderly, with the largest increase in drugs not yet approved and in approved drugs tested in new diseases. We document an increase in drug utilization of newly tested drugs among elderly individuals and analyze trial results, adverse events, and drug approvals. Our findings show how financial incentives can increase representation in product development and shift the rate, direction, and adoption of innovation to potentially benefit underserved groups.

papers.title: Regional Variations and Productivity Puzzles in Health Care
papers.abstract: Health care utilization per capita varies widely across the United States, yet higher utilization areas have no better patient health. In the late 2000s, this pattern was widely interpreted as evidence that health care costs could be cut substantially without harming patients, which in turn shaped the 2010 Affordable Care Act. We describe how our understanding has since evolved, emphasizing three points. First, new evidence indicates quantitatively meaningful roles for both supply-side and demand-side factors in driving regional variation in health care and in health outcomes. Second, health care productivity varies substantially across providers; improving it requires better understanding of why productivity differs. Third, we know even less about the sources of area-level productivity differences. We suggest several ways in which greater engagement with the productivity literature outside of health care could yield valuable insights.
